The gap is that the trace lacks a duration field per call. Adding wall-clock latency per request would establish whether the document fetch had time to complete.
The gap is that the response content is not stored. Storing the full response text is sufficient, because anything the model saw must have come from the response.
There is no gap. If the wrapper logged the tool result, that is the content the model received, because the wrapper is the component that assembles the request.

questions.explanation: The distinction is between logging an intent and logging the artefact, and only one of them is evidence. The wrapper is where a tool result is handled, so a log at that point records what the wrapper held — which is not necessarily what ended up in the `messages` array, because content can be truncated, filtered, re-serialised or stripped in between, and any content-block filtering is exactly what breaks thinking-block replay as well. The trace that supports an investigation has to be the request as assembled: the complete `messages` array including every `tool_use` id and matching `tool_result`, plus the model, `max_tokens` and the temperature and effort settings; and on the response side the `stop_reason`, the full `content` blocks and the `usage` breakdown with cache read, cache creation and output tokens. Add the `request_id` and it is reproducible verbatim, which is the standard the compliance and support cases actually need. Duration and response-only logging are both real signals, but neither answers the question that was asked here.

whyWrong.B: It proposes a plausible metric that cannot answer the question. Latency tells you whether a call was slow; it cannot tell you whether the content in the request was what the wrapper logged.
whyWrong.C: It stores the wrong side of the exchange. The allegation is about what was sent, so the request is the artefact that has to be recorded; the response alone cannot show what the model was given.
whyWrong.D: It assumes no transformation occurs between the wrapper and the request. Content-block handling is where thinking-block replay breaks, which is direct evidence that this stage is not a pass-through.

questions.mindset: Evidence is the request as assembled — full `messages`, model, parameters, plus `stop_reason`, content and `usage` — because the wrapper's view can diverge from the bytes sent.

questions.scenario: Ironbridge's extraction loop uses structured outputs with `output_config.format`. Three records come back with `stop_reason: max_tokens`, three with `stop_reason: refusal`, and three valid objects whose every field is an empty string. Only the middle group is being retried.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about handling these three groups are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: The two `max_tokens` cases need a clean resend: with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` the output may be incomplete and simply not match your schema, so retry with a higher `max_tokens` — resending the original request cleanly with a fresh message history, or using the documented continuation approach, so you never accumulate two candidate extractions in one conversation.

The empty-but-valid objects are a content problem that no amount of schema work addresses. Structured outputs guarantee the shape of the response, not that its values are populated, so an object whose every field is an empty string is schema-valid and semantically useless. It needs an application-level acceptance check — a per-field non-empty requirement for fields the business depends on, with an explicit nullable or sentinel representation for genuine absence so that 'the document did not contain it' is expressible rather than being indistinguishable from a failed extraction.
The refusal cases should be retried identically, because a refusal is a safety condition that resolves on a subsequent attempt once the model's sampling has moved on.

All three groups are schema failures and one fix covers them: raise `max_tokens` so no response is truncated, and add an explicit prompt instruction telling the model never to refuse and never to return empty fields.

questions.explanation: Grouping these three together is the mistake, because they need three different responses and only one of them is a schema problem. Truncation: with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` the output may be incomplete and simply not match your schema; the fix is a higher `max_tokens`, resent cleanly with a fresh message history or via the documented continuation approach, so you never end up with two candidate extractions in one conversation. Refusal: a 200 with `stop_reason: "refusal"` may not match your schema at all, because the refusal message takes precedence over schema constraints — that one needs the request adjusted or a fallback model, never an identical retry, which is why retrying the middle group as written is wrong. Emptiness: the guarantee is about shape, so a fully-populated object with empty values passes every schema check and still carries no information. That is an acceptance problem, and the durable fix is to make absence representable — nullable or an explicit sentinel — so that a document genuinely lacking a field and a failed extraction stop looking the same.

whyWrong.C: It treats a refusal as transient. A refusal is a deliberate condition that takes precedence over schema constraints, so an identical retry re-reads the same request and is at best a source of spend.
whyWrong.D: It applies one remedy to three different causes. Only the truncated cases respond to a higher limit; a prompt instruction cannot make absence representable, and promising the model never to refuse simply relocates the failure outside your visibility.

questions.mindset: Truncation gets a clean resend, refusal gets an adjusted request, and a valid-but-empty object gets an acceptance check — only one of the three is a schema failure.

questions.scenario: Ironbridge's adjudicator has a 30-second end-to-end latency budget per claim. During a 529 incident the retry helper runs five attempts with exponential backoff, and the p99 climbs to four minutes while only a handful of claims succeed.
questions.stem: What is the wrong parameterisation, and what should bound the retries instead?

options.text: Attempt count is the wrong bound because it says nothing about wall-clock. Bounding retries by both an attempt cap and a total time budget lets the run terminate with a recorded reason, and jitter keeps the surviving retries from re-arriveing as a wave. With a 30-second budget, the correct behaviour is to stop early, record the attempt count, elapsed time and the last error class, and route the claim to a queued or dead-letter path so the latency SLO holds and the work is not lost. The distinction from a circuit breaker is scope: a breaker stops sending entirely after a threshold and admits probe requests after a cooldown, which is the right tool when every request in the fleet is being hit, whereas a per-request time budget is right when the pipeline must keep answering inside its own SLO.
Attempt count is exactly the right bound. Reducing it to two attempts brings the p99 inside the 30-second budget without needing any concept of elapsed time.
Retries should be removed entirely during a 529 and every claim failed over to a fallback model, because a degraded-model answer is preferable to a slow one.
The latency budget is the wrong instrument. Report the 529s and let the upstream gateway handle retries, since it can be configured with a deadline.

questions.explanation: Two budgets were being confused. An attempt cap bounds work per call; a total time budget bounds what the caller experiences, and only the second one can protect a 30-second SLO — five attempts at growing intervals can occupy four minutes while still being 'only five'. The documented discipline is to bound both attempts and total elapsed time, with exponential backoff and jitter so the attempts do not synchronise into a wave, and to make an exhausted budget a distinct recorded outcome rather than a generic failure — so the runbook can tell a budget stop from a network fault. What happens then is a design choice with a cost: route the claim to a queued or dead-letter path rather than dropping it, which is what keeps the SLO intact without losing work. The adjacent tool is a circuit breaker, and it operates at a different scope — after a threshold of consecutive failures it opens and fails fast without touching the network, returning a distinguishable provider-unavailable signal, and after a cooldown it admits limited probe requests. That is the right answer when the whole fleet is being hit; a per-request time budget is right when your own SLO is the binding constraint.

whyWrong.B: It treats attempts as a latency control. Two attempts at long intervals can still exceed the budget, and capping attempts alone says nothing about how long a single attempt is permitted to take.
whyWrong.C: It trades correctness of record for latency without being asked to. Degrading to a fallback model changes the answer for every claim in the incident, which is a decision that belongs in the recovery matrix rather than in an incident response.
whyWrong.D: It externalises a constraint you already own. Relying on a gateway deadline gives up the ability to record the attempt count, elapsed time and last error class that make the budget stop diagnosable.

questions.mindset: Bound retries by attempts *and* elapsed time, record which budget stopped the run, and queue rather than drop — a breaker is a fleet-scope tool, not an SLO tool.

questions.scenario: Ironbridge fixed an integration defect that dropped older turns from the `messages` array. The team wants a permanent guard, and a proposal is on the table: add the captured failing case to the suite and have an LLM judge score whether the response is correct.
questions.stem: Which assessment of that proposal is correct?

options.text: The grader is the problem. A regression test for a message-construction defect has an unambiguous expected outcome — the response must be based on the history that was sent — so it belongs with a deterministic grader that asserts a property of the request or the output, and it runs on every change. Model graders earn their place where there is no ground truth, and you earn the right to use one by calibrating it against human labels and measuring its run-to-run variance, so that a small movement can be told from noise. Add the deterministic assertion as the guard; keep an LLM judge, if you have one, for the qualities it can actually see.
The proposal is sound. An LLM judge is the most sensitive detector of a dropped-turn defect, because it can recognise that an answer ignores earlier context even when no exact string assertion would.
The proposal is sound but should be graded by a different model family than the one under test, so the grader does not share blind spots with the system.
Neither a deterministic assertion nor a judge is reliable here. The only trustworthy guard is a production monitor, since the defect was invisible until it happened in production.

questions.explanation: The right question is what kind of success this case has, and a dropped-turn defect has the simplest possible one: the request either contains the prior turns or it does not. That is a property of the request, checkable by an assertion, deterministic, and cheap enough to run on every change — which is exactly what a regression guard has to be. Handing it to an LLM judge makes it strictly weaker and strictly noisier, because the judge brings its own run-to-run variance on top of the signal, and you then have to calibrate it against human labels and measure that variance before a small movement means anything. The docs' stated best practice reinforces the split: grade with a different model from the one generating the output, since a same-family grader shares blind spots with the system under test. That is an argument for using a judge well — on qualities with no ground truth — not an argument for choosing a judge where a ground truth exists. And a production monitor is not a substitute: it detects the recurrence after it has shipped, which is the thing the guard was supposed to prevent.

whyWrong.B: It argues for the least sensitive detector. A deterministic assertion on the request catches the defect on every run, while a judge adds variance to a signal that was already exactly checkable.
whyWrong.C: It keeps the grader as a judge and only swaps the family. Cross-family grading is good practice for judging, but it does not remove the noise or the fact that this case had a deterministic expected outcome available.
whyWrong.D: It abandons pre-ship detection. A monitor tells you the defect returned after deployment; a deterministic case in the suite tells you before it does, which is the entire value of turning an incident into an eval case.

questions.mindset: Grade with a model only where there is no ground truth; a dropped-turn defect has an exact expected outcome and belongs to a deterministic assertion.
